newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin backs Russian PM's government reform plan.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin backs Russian PM's government reform plan.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin on Tuesday backed Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin's plan to restructure his government and scotched rumours that the premier himself might lose his job in the near future.
Yeltsin, who wants to reassert his authority after a long illness, also scolded Russia's chief prosecutor for a series of humiliating failures in the fight against organised crime.

Kremlin spokesman Sergei Yastrzhembsky said Yeltsin, whose criticism of the government last week triggered speculation about Chernomyrdin's future, discussed ways of improving the cabinet's work in his Kremlin talks with the prime minister.
"Viktor Stepanovich (Chernomyrdin) described his vision of a structural reorganisation of the cabinet of ministers and of the appropriate personnel changes," Yastrzhembsky told a news briefing.
"Boris Nikolayevich (Yeltsin) fully approved the plan," he added.
Yastrzhembsky said Yeltsin, back in the Kremlin after eight months fighting heart problems and then pneumonia, also discussed with Chernomyrdin specific personnel changes.

The spokesman did not say which ministers would be involved in the reshuffle, but said an announcement would be made at a cabinet meeting set for Thursday after Yeltsin has made his annual address to parliament.
Yastrzhembsky made clear that there was no immediate threat to the premier himself, saying Yeltsin had approved a schedule of foreign trips for Chernomyrdin stretching into May.
Chernomyrdin, a symbol of political stability and continuing reforms for the outside world, will visit China, the Czech Republic and Slovakia, Yastrzhembsky said.

Political experts have said that changes in the government are most likely to affect ministers dealing with the economy and social policy and possibly Defence Minister Igor Rodionov, who was given a dressing down by Yeltsin last week.

Speculation has also centred on whether Anatoly Chubais, the influential chief of the Kremlin staff and an instigator of market reforms in Russia, will be given a formal role in the government to oversee the economy.
Yeltsin, 66, looked in good form in brief television footage of him greeting Chernomyrdin, who is a loyal ally but has been under fire over the failure to pay wages in the state sector.

The president chided Chernomyrdin last week but his main aim may have been to create the impression that he is firmly in charge and means to tackle the economic and political problems that have piled up during his absence from the Kremlin.

Yeltsin also had talks with Prosecutor-General Yuri Skuratov. Russian television showed Yeltsin criticising Skuratov, who stared in silence at the president as he sat across the table from him in the Kremlin.
Yeltsin said he was dissatisfied with his work and warned him that public anger was rising over his failure to solve a growing list of high-profile murders.
"Behind the overall figures, which I am well acquainted with, are hidden some prominent murders which the whole of society is seething about," Interfax quoted Yeltsin as saying.

Crime, much of it involving mafia-style gangs, has risen sharply since the Soviet Union collapsed in 1991. Skuratov has been ridiculed by the media for failing to solve any of the prominent murder cases.
Crime is expected to be one of the main themes in Yeltsin's parliamentary address on Thursday, in which he will set out his policies for the year ahead.
The speech, expected to last 40 minutes, will be his longest public appearance since he fell ill before his re-election last July and is seen as a test of his recovery and ability to rule.
